reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: if (!carrier.isPending) { carrier.isPending = true; pending.push(carrier) } — drained as an array
reading.floor: pendingSet.add(carrier) — drained by iterating the Set and clearing it
reading.caveat: ONE OPERATION IS ONE MARK. A frame marks every carrier the stated number of times, in passes over the whole population, and then drains, so a repeat mark is the flag's early return on ours and a hash hit on the Set. The drain runs one counting body per carrier on both arms and both were checked to run the same number before the clock. This is the shape of `OIMChannel.enlist` and its frame loop, hand-written, so one carrier shape reaches each arm; production carriers are megamorphic there, which charges the field reads on our side and not the Set on the other, so the ratio is a lower bound on what the flag costs in the engine.

reading.ours: a delivery list built at the write — the frame walks only what was marked
reading.floor: a stamp written at the write — the frame scans every subscriber for this frame's stamp
reading.caveat: ONE OPERATION IS ONE FRAME: the stated number of subscribers out of the population are marked, spread evenly, and the frame delivers to exactly those. So the answer turns on the marked fraction and THE ROWS CROSS OVER: read them as a table, never as one ratio. Both arms were checked to deliver to the same number of subscribers before the clock.

reading.ours: mark the node at the write, recompute each marked node once when the frame closes
reading.floor: recompute the node at every write
reading.caveat: ONE OPERATION IS ONE FRAME over the whole node population, each node taking the stated number of writes to its sources. reading.ours: compare the leaf's frame stamp, write it, push onto the frame array — no arrival is a repeat
reading.floor: add the leaf to the frame's Set, which dedups by containment — no arrival is a repeat
reading.caveat: THE ROW WITH NOTHING TO DEDUPLICATE, AND IT IS HERE BECAUSE IT IS THE ONE THE STAMP SHOULD WIN LEAST. Every leaf reads one root, so all 200 arrivals of a frame are first arrivals: our stamp never takes its early return and the `Set` never probes an entry it already holds. What is left in the difference is a field compare plus a field store plus an array push against one hash insert, with no repeat path exercised on either side. A reader who wants to know what the stamp is worth when the graph is a tree — one consumer per root, which is what most screens are — reads this row and not the other two. It is also the row that says whether the recovered figures can be quoted at all: if the stamp does not lead here, the mechanism is not what the quoted per-arrival numbers were describing. RESIDUALS. WHAT THE `Set` BUYS, and it is not nothing: dedup and containment are ONE operation, there is no per-leaf word to keep in step, and the invariant the stamp design holds by hand — a leaf is on the frame's list iff its stamp says so — cannot be broken, so that arm cannot list a leaf twice or lose one. The stamp buys back two things the `Set` cannot: it is a FRAME NUMBER, so it is stale again at the next frame with nobody clearing it, and it is also the DETACH — a leaf let go of between the write that listed it and the flush is unlisted by writing the same field, and the frame's pass reads it again before calling. A `Set` design needs a second mechanism for that and this arm is not charged for one. WHAT THE ENGINE DOES TODAY IS NEITHER ARM AS PRICED: `TOIMEffect.isRunScheduled` is a BOOLEAN, which the frame's pass clears as it consumes a leaf and `detach` writes false — the same compare and store, so the operation count here stands, and the self-staling property this arm is credited with is one the boolean does not have. The row is a reading of the frame-number arm and owes a run against the boolean [NO RUN BEHIND THIS FIGURE]. AGAINST US: our arm carries a frame number and pays a compare and a store the `Set` arm does not, because the stamp is doing the queue's dedup as well as its own. AGAINST THE `Set` ARM: its `clear()` is proportional to what it held where our `length = 0` is not, and both are inside the operation count here rather than hidden outside it. WHAT NEITHER ARM PAYS: the write that produced the arrival and the walk of `slot.effects` that carried it, which are `OIMChannel.write`'s and identical on both sides.

reading.floor: rows.set(key, row) — and skip an identity map that is still empty
reading.caveat: A FIRST LOAD INTO AN EMPTY STORE, THE ROW THE TWO-MAP SHAPE WINS. Ours mints a slot per row and files it; the floor files the bare row and tests the identity map's size, which is zero, so it mints nothing. Both stores are rebuilt between passes, untimed, and the minted slots are collected outside the clock. Above one is expected and is the case for the rejected shape; read it with the overwrite row.

reading.floor: rows.get(key)
reading.caveat: ONE INDIRECTION MORE ON OUR SIDE: the row sits on the slot, so a read by key is a hash and a field load where the two-map store answers with the hash alone. reading.floor: rows.set(key, row); then identities.get(key) because that map is no longer empty
reading.caveat: WHERE THE BILL FOR TWO MAPS ARRIVES. One subscriber stands on one key, mounted before the clock, so the identity map is not empty and EVERY write on the floor pays a second hash to learn whether its key is watched; ours resolved the slot with the one hash it needed to write, and the subscriber list is a field on it. Exactly one write per pass lands on the watched row and is delivered on both sides, so the difference is the per-row probe and not the delivery. Ours transcribes the prefix of `OIMChannel.writeWithoutFlushCheck` — `slot.effects`, the stamp against the frame, the `isPending` enlist and the stamp store — without the clock wrap and the flush request; the floor is the self-contained emitter the post turned down, one hash to find the handlers and one string-`Set` insertion to dedup the key. reading.floor: the same move, membership in a list kept in the caller's order (OIMBucketSlotsServiceArrayDriven)
reading.caveat: A BUCKET OF 100, and the size is in the id because the answer is a function of it on BOTH halves. THE COUNT THIS PREDICTS, per member moved, through `bucketCollection.writeContent`: on the ordered half, `reconcile` compares the held list against the one handed in up to the swapped band, finds them unequal, drains all 100 members and pushes all 100 back, and the collection holds 100 arrivals and unholds 100 departures. reading.caveat: THE COUNTERWEIGHT TO THE ROW ABOVE, AND IT IS OWED. An unchanged re-send is the one write on which the shipped walk allocates nothing whatever, so measuring the rejected design only there would report its worst case as its case. Here every write moves all sixteen columns: BOTH arms allocate a changed-names array and push sixteen names into it, both assign sixteen columns, and both mark the row and its columns. The floor's names array is then one allocation among several rather than its only one, and if the shipped walk's advantage is really the allocation, this ratio is markedly closer to 1.00 than the unchanged row's. ONE OPERATION IS ONE `updateEntity` CARRYING SIXTEEN COLUMNS. The values advance by one of eight per pass and column `c` takes `titles[(round + c) & 7]`, so no write is ever handed a value the row already holds. THE WRITE AROUND THE WALK IS IDENTICAL ON BOTH ARMS AND IS INSIDE BOTH NUMBERS: `assertWritable` with the channel's `assertNotFlushing`, `openSubframe`/`closeSubframe`, the writer dispatch, the `length > 0` test, and — on a write that moves something — the changed-names array, `markColumnsChanged`'s column-store probe per moved column, `channel.writeWithoutFlushCheck` and `markContentChanged`. That is a large constant added to the numerator and the denominator alike, so it pulls this ratio toward 1.00 and the printed ratio is a LOWER BOUND on the difference between the two walks. The two nanosecond columns beside it are not pulled anywhere: subtract them to get the per-write difference the row is actually about. THIS PAIR DECLARES `isolate`, AND THE READING IS UNINTERPRETABLE WITHOUT IT. Both arms reach the engine through one compiled function — `OIMEntityCollection.prototype.patchEntity`, whose single call site `this.entityWriter.patchEntity(entitySlot, patch)` would see both writers in one process.
